stages.title: Advanced drawing and composition
stages.hook: Why does a diagonal line in a picture feel more dramatic than a horizontal one?
explain: Strong compositions are planned. Artists make small thumbnail sketches to test layouts before committing. Values (lights and darks) are grouped into a few large masses so the picture reads clearly from a distance, even before detail is added.

Compositional tools guide the eye. Leading lines such as roads, arms or rivers point toward the focal point. Horizontal lines feel stable, vertical lines feel upright, and diagonals suggest movement or tension. Repetition creates rhythm, and variation prevents monotony. Negative space gives rest.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is often used as a proportion guide. Two quantities are in the golden ratio if the whole divided by the larger part equals the larger part divided by the smaller. Many claims that famous works use it are debated, and it is a tool rather than a law. Compositional traditions vary, such as Chinese paintings that leave large empty areas on purpose.

example.q: Divide a 100 cm line into two parts in the golden ratio. How long is the larger part (nearest 0.1 cm)?

analogies.sport: A football play uses diagonal passes to create tension.
analogies.tech: Interface designers use hierarchy and white space to direct attention.

stages.mnemonic: Plan small, group the values, lead the eye, leave it room to breathe.

misc.right: The golden ratio is one possible guide. Its role in famous artworks is often exaggerated, and good composition depends on purpose.

stages.title: Oil painting
stages.hook: Why can an oil painting be reworked for days while an acrylic one is dry in minutes?
explain: Oil paint is pigment ground in a drying oil, most often linseed oil. It dries slowly by oxidation, which means taking up oxygen from the air, not by evaporating water. Surfaces become touch-dry in days and may take months to cure fully.

The rule "fat over lean" means each upper layer should contain more oil than the layer below, so the lower layers dry first and do not crack the upper ones. Techniques include alla prima (finishing in one wet session), glazing (thin transparent layers over a dry layer for depth and glow), and impasto (thick, textured paint). Solvents such as odourless mineral spirits must be used with ventilation and kept away from flames; oils on rags can heat and ignite, so rags are disposed of safely.

Oil painting became dominant in Europe in the 1400s, with Flemish painters such as Jan van Eyck. Before that, tempera and fresco were common, and other regions used their own paints such as ink, gouache or acrylic later. Painters in Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia use oil today.

example.q: A painter uses 1 part oil in the first layer and 2 parts oil in the second. Does this follow fat over lean?
steps: The top layer has more oil (2 > 1).
Fat over lean means more oil on top.

stages.title: Advanced colour relationships
stages.hook: Put the same grey square on a blue and then on an orange background. Does it look the same?
explain: Colour has three dimensions: hue (the colour family), value (lightness) and saturation or chroma (intensity). Colours also affect each other: this is simultaneous contrast, described by the French chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul in 1839. A grey looks slightly warmer on blue and cooler on orange, because the eye exaggerates differences.

Colour harmonies are plans: monochromatic (one hue), analogous (neighbours), complementary (opposites), split-complementary (one hue plus the two beside its complement), and triadic (three evenly spaced hues). Temperature adds another layer, as warm colours tend to advance and cool ones recede. Josef Albers explored these effects in Interaction of Color (1963).

Light and pigment mix differently. Screens use additive RGB (red, green, blue light), where all together make white. Printing uses subtractive mixing, such as cyan, magenta and yellow, where mixing darkens. Colour meanings differ between cultures, so artists check context.

example.q: What hue is complementary to purple on the traditional painter's wheel?
steps: So purple and yellow are complementary.

analogies.home: A neutral grey sofa looks different next to a bright orange cushion.
analogies.city: Shop signs use contrasting colours to attract attention.

stages.title: Renaissance art
stages.hook: Why did painters in Italy around 1400 suddenly start making flat walls look like deep rooms?
explain: The Renaissance means "rebirth" and refers to a period in Europe from about the 1300s to the 1600s, beginning in Italian cities like Florence. Artists studied classical Greek and Roman art, the natural world and human anatomy. Humanism, interest in human life and learning, shaped many works.

Technical advances included linear perspective, demonstrated by Brunelleschi in the early 1400s and described by Leon Battista Alberti around 1435. Artists also used chiaroscuro and sfumato (soft blending). Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa from about 1503. Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1508 to 1512. Raphael painted The School of Athens around 1509 to 1511. Sofonisba Anguissola and Titian were also important.

In northern Europe, painters such as Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer perfected oil painting and printmaking. The Renaissance was not the only creative era of its time: Benin artists cast brass plaques in the 1500s and 1600s, Mughal painters developed court miniature painting, and Ming dynasty artists worked in China. Many historians now see the Renaissance as one important thread among many.

example.q: The Sistine Chapel ceiling was painted from 1508 to 1512. How many years did it take?
steps: The span is about four years.
Check: it was a large project completed in a short time.

analogies.music: Renaissance musicians and painters shared the same humanist interest in harmony and proportion.

stages.title: Impressionism and Expressionism
stages.hook: How can a painting show a feeling, or the flicker of light, better than a photograph can?
explain: Impressionism began in France in the 1860s and 1870s. Painters like Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt painted everyday scenes and changing light with quick brushstrokes and bright colour. The name came from Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872) after a group exhibition in 1874. Many painted outdoors (en plein air). Japanese woodblock prints influenced several of them.

Expressionism, early 1900s in Germany and Austria, wanted to show inner feeling rather than outward appearance. Edvard Munch painted The Scream in 1893, an important forerunner. Die Brücke formed in Dresden in 1905, and Der Blaue Reiter formed in Munich in 1911 with Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. Artists used distorted forms and strong colour. Käthe Kollwitz made powerful prints about human suffering.

The two movements ask different questions. Impressionism asks how light looks to the eye at a moment. Expressionism asks what the world feels like inside. Both broke with strict academic realism, and both are part of wider global modernisms.

example.a: How light and colour change with time

stages.title: Cubism and Surrealism
stages.hook: What if you could show a face from the front and the side at the same time? What would it look like?
explain: Cubism began in Paris around 1907 to 1908 with Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque. Instead of one viewpoint, they broke objects into planes and showed several angles at once. Analytic Cubism (about 1909 to 1912) used muted browns and greys and fragmented forms. Synthetic Cubism (from about 1912) used brighter colour and collage, which means gluing paper or objects onto the work. Picasso and others also studied African masks and sculpture, a debt that is now more openly acknowledged.

Surrealism was launched by André Breton's manifesto in 1924. It explored dreams and the unconscious. Techniques included automatism (spontaneous drawing without planning) and unexpected juxtaposition (putting unrelated things together). Salvador Dalí, René Magritte, Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo are well-known Surrealists. Magritte's The Treachery of Images (1929) reminds us a painting of a pipe is not a pipe.

Frida Kahlo is often linked with Surrealism, but she said she painted her own reality. Surrealism spread internationally, including to Latin America and Africa, where artists developed their own versions.

example.q: Cubist artists show a guitar from the front, side and top in one picture. What problem do they challenge?
steps: They challenge the idea of one fixed view.
example.a: The idea that a picture must show one fixed viewpoint

analogies.tech: A 3D model viewed from many sides is like a Cubist idea.

stages.title: Sculpture and three-dimensional design
stages.hook: What makes a sculpture stay up, feel heavy or feel light? Try balancing objects to find out.
explain: Three-dimensional design deals with mass (solid parts), void (empty spaces), balance, scale and surface. Sculptors think about how a work looks from every side, how it sits in space, and how viewers move around it.

Most sculpture begins with planning. A maquette is a small preliminary model. An armature is an internal frame, often wire, that supports soft material like clay. Scale models help with big works: a 1:10 maquette is one tenth of the final size. Balance can be symmetrical (mirrored) or asymmetrical (visual weight balanced). Pioneers include Constantin Brancusi, who simplified forms, Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth, who used holes and open forms, and Alexander Calder, whose balanced mobiles from the 1930s move with air.

Traditions around the world use mass and void in different ways. Benin bronze cast figures, Chinese Han dynasty ceramic figures, and Dogon carved wooden figures from Mali each have their own design languages.

example.q: A maquette is 15 cm tall at a scale of 1:10. How tall is the final work?

stages.title: Global artistic traditions
stages.hook: If you could put art from five continents on one wall, what would help you compare them fairly?
explain: Fair comparison starts with asking the same questions of every work: who made it, for whom, from what, and for what purpose. Art is made for many reasons: worship, decoration, record, power, play. No tradition is a "primitive" stage on the way to another.

Examples: The Kingdom of Benin (in present-day Nigeria) cast brass plaques in the 1500s and 1600s for the royal palace. Islamic art uses calligraphy and geometric pattern in places like the Alhambra in Spain. Mughal court painters in South Asia produced detailed miniatures. Chinese ink painting and Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints developed rich traditions. Indigenous Australian art includes ancient rock art and contemporary acrylic painting. Maya and Inca artists made monumental stone carving and fine textiles. Māori carvers of Aotearoa New Zealand decorate meeting houses with story-bearing carving. Kente cloth is woven by the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana.

Many works are linked to living communities. Respectful study involves learning names of artists where known, correct terms, and listening to the communities. Museums face questions about returning works taken in colonial times.

example.q: Both Benin plaques and Mughal miniatures served royal courts. Is that a similarity or a difference?
steps: Note the shared function: courts commissioned art.

example.a: A similarity in purpose, with different materials

stages.title: Digital illustration and painting
stages.hook: What can a digital canvas do that paper cannot, and what can paper do that a screen cannot?
explain: Digital art is made with software and a tablet, mouse or touchscreen. Raster images are made of pixels (tiny coloured squares), so they lose sharpness when enlarged. Vector images use mathematical paths, so they can scale to any size without losing quality.

Layers act like transparent sheets, so you can paint, edit and hide parts without changing others. Blend modes mix layers in different ways. Non-destructive work keeps originals safe. Image resolution is measured in pixels per inch (ppi) or dots per inch (dpi) for print. Print size = pixels ÷ ppi. Screens use RGB colour, and printers often use CMYK, so colours can shift.

File formats matter: PNG is lossless and good for graphics, JPEG is lossy and smaller, and SVG stores vector shapes. Digital artists still use traditional principles: composition, value, colour and drawing. Keep backups, and credit sources when using references. Artists worldwide use digital tools from Lagos to Seoul to São Paulo.
